lessons.title: The confusion matrix, precision/recall and ROC vs PR
lessons.intro: Every classifier answer in an interview starts with 'which metric, and why?'. Four counts (TP, FP, FN, TN) generate precision, recall, F1 and both curves; the skill is knowing which of them your data and your costs make meaningful.
takeaways: Precision and recall ignore true negatives; accuracy is dominated by them when classes are imbalanced.
F1 is a harmonic mean; F-beta shifts the weight toward recall (beta > 1) or precision (beta < 1).
On rare classes the false-positive rate hides the cost of false alarms; PR curves show it. A random scorer's PR-AUC is the prevalence.
ROC-AUC is invariant to monotone score transforms and measures ranking only; the operating threshold comes from the cost matrix.
lessons.trap: Quoting one headline number (accuracy or AUC) for an imbalanced problem, without a threshold, a base rate or a cost.

sections.heading: Four counts, three ratios
sections.text: Precision, recall and F1 never use the true negatives. When negatives are plentiful that is a feature: a large TN count cannot flatter them, whereas accuracy is mostly TN.
code: p, r = tp / (tp + fp), tp / (tp + fn)

sections.heading: A positive result and the base rate
sections.text: With 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity, a positive test for a 0.1% condition is wrong 9 times out of 10. This is Bayes' rule on a confusion matrix, and it is the most common 'why is precision so low?' answer.

sections.heading: AUC is a ranking probability
sections.text: ROC-AUC is the share of positive-negative pairs that are ordered correctly, so squashing scores with any increasing function leaves it unchanged. It says nothing about which threshold to use.
code: auc = lambda p, n: float((p[:, None] > n[None, :]).mean())

sections.heading: Choose the threshold from costs
sections.text: Sweep thresholds and total the cost of errors. When a miss costs ten times a false alarm the cheapest operating point moves to a lower threshold.
code: cost = lambda t, cfn: ((s < t) & (y == 1)).sum() * cfn + ((s >= t) & (y == 0)).sum()
print('equal costs:', round(float(ths[np.argmin([cost(t, 1) for t in ths])]), 2))
print('miss costs 10x:', round(float(ths[np.argmin([cost(t, 10) for t in ths])]), 2))

lessons.title: Calibration, splits and significance
lessons.intro: A metric is only as trustworthy as the experiment behind it. This lesson is the checklist for probabilities you can act on, splits that mimic production, and differences that are bigger than noise.
takeaways: Calibration (reliability diagram, ECE) is separate from ranking quality; recalibrate with a monotone map fitted on held-out data.
Split the way production will: by time for forecasting, by group when rows are correlated, and fit every transform inside the training part.
Report an interval, not just a point: standard error is about sqrt(p(1-p)/n), and peeking at a p-value inflates false positives.
Offline metrics are filters; the randomised online experiment measures the outcome.
lessons.trap: Comparing two models by a single test-set number and a 'higher is better' eyeball, with no error bar, no group split and no calibration check.

sections.heading: Calibration: the number must mean something
sections.text: Group predictions by confidence and compare with the observed hit rate. A model that says 0.9 but is right 60% of the time is over-confident, even when its ranking (AUC) is excellent.

sections.heading: A random split can flatter a time series
sections.text: On a trending series, shuffled folds put neighbouring points in train and test, so a model that simply copies the nearest neighbour looks accurate. Splitting by time asks the real question.
code: near = lambda tr, te: np.mean([abs(y[i] - y[tr[np.argmin(abs(tr - i))]]) for i in te])
sections.output:
random split MAE 0.29
time split MAE   1.02

sections.heading: Is the difference real?
sections.text: Two models 1 point apart on 400 examples are inside the sampling noise. Estimate the standard error of the difference before celebrating, and prefer paired comparisons on the same examples.

lessons.title: Ranking and regression metrics
lessons.intro: Search, recommendation and retrieval (the heart of RAG) are judged by ranked lists, not labels. Regression has its own traps. Pick the metric that matches how the output is consumed.
takeaways: Retrieval for RAG: recall@k says whether the answer reached the model; MRR and nDCG say how early.
MAE is a typical error in the target's units; RMSE punishes outliers; MAPE is unstable near zero.
Negative R^2 means worse than predicting the mean.
Always state k and the relevance definition when quoting a ranking metric.
lessons.trap: Optimising nDCG@10 offline and never checking that users look past the first two results.

sections.heading: Precision@k, recall@k, MRR, nDCG
sections.text: P@k and recall@k look only at set membership in the top k. MRR rewards the first hit. nDCG uses graded relevance with a log discount, so order matters most near the top.

sections.heading: MAE, RMSE and MAPE disagree for a reason
sections.text: One large error moves RMSE far more than MAE. MAPE explodes for small targets. R^2 compares to the mean predictor and can be negative.
